title: Pixels, Replay, and the Moving Target: Reconstructing the First Atari DQN
summary: The paper combines convolutional action-value prediction, experience replay, and off-policy Q-learning to learn control from Atari pixels across seven games.
prerequisites: Basic probability, especially expectations and conditional expectations
Neural-network function approximation and stochastic gradient updates
Reinforcement-learning concepts: states, actions, rewards, policies, and discounted returns
objectives: Define discounted return, optimal action value, the Bellman target, and the Q-network loss
Explain why the agent uses four processed frames and emits one value per legal action
Trace the interaction, replay, random-minibatch, update, and epsilon-greedy action loop
Interpret each reported comparison under its actual training and evaluation conditions
Distinguish observed training stability from a theoretical convergence guarantee

sections.title: The control problem concealed by the screen
sections.markdown:
An Atari agent is not handed variables such as “ball velocity” or “remaining oxygen.” At time $t$, it selects an action $a_t$ from the legal set $\mathcal A=\{1,\ldots,K\}$, observes an image $x_t\in\mathbb R^d$, receives reward $r_t$, and may eventually receive a terminal signal. The environment $\mathcal E$ has an internal state, but that state is hidden from the learner. In the paper's formulation, reward represents the change in game score, and useful feedback may follow an action only after a long delay.

A single screen can also be ambiguous. A still image may show an object without revealing its direction of travel. The paper therefore defines the formal state as the complete interaction history
$$s_t=(x_1,a_1,x_2,\ldots,a_{t-1},x_t).$$
Here $s_t$ includes every observation through $x_t$ and every earlier action. Treating each finite history as a distinct state yields a very large finite Markov decision process. It does not, however, make an arbitrarily long sequence practical as neural-network input. The implemented system instead applies a function $\phi$ to make a fixed-length representation from four recent processed frames.

That distinction prevents a common conceptual slip: $s_t$ is the paper's formal history state, whereas $\phi(s_t)$ is the bounded representation actually fed to DQN. The learning problem is therefore more than image classification. Visual features must support decisions under delayed scalar rewards, correlated observations, partial observability, and a training distribution that changes as the agent changes its behavior.

sections.title: The promise encoded by an action value
sections.markdown:
Define the discounted return beginning at time $t$ by
$$R_t=\sum_{t'=t}^{T}\gamma^{t'-t}r_{t'},$$
where $T$ is the terminal time, $t'$ indexes reward times, $r_{t'}$ is the reward at $t'$, and $\gamma$ is the per-step discount factor. The optimal action-value $Q^*(s,a)$ is the largest expected return available after observing history $s$, taking action $a$, and then following an optimal policy $\pi$. A policy maps histories to actions or action distributions.

The Bellman equation expresses this value recursively:
$$Q^*(s,a)=\mathbb E_{s'\sim\mathcal E}\!\left[r+\gamma\max_{a'}Q^*(s',a')\mid s,a\right].$$
Here $s'$ is the next history sampled through environment dynamics, $r$ is the immediate reward, and $a'$ ranges over legal next actions. The maximum represents control: after reaching $s'$, value the best available continuation.

**Illustrative arithmetic.** Suppose a sampled transition has $r=1$, $\gamma=0.9$, and estimated next-action values $Q(s',\cdot)=(2,4,3)$. The one-step target is
$$y=1+0.9\max(2,4,3)=1+3.6=4.6.$$
If the current prediction is $Q(s,a;\theta)=3.1$, its sampled squared error is
$$(y-Q(s,a;\theta))^2=(4.6-3.1)^2=2.25.$$
These numbers are invented solely to demonstrate the calculation; they are not measurements from Atari.

A Q-value does not predict only the next change in score. It estimates discounted cumulative return. Immediate reward is one term; the bootstrapped next-state value estimates what may follow.

sections.title: Learning from labels that learning itself moves
sections.markdown:
At iteration $i$, the paper describes the squared-error objective
$$L_i(\theta_i)=\mathbb E_{s,a\sim\rho}\left[(y_i-Q(s,a;\theta_i))^2\right],$$
with target
$$y_i=\mathbb E_{s'\sim\mathcal E}\left[r+\gamma\max_{a'}Q(s',a';\theta_{i-1})\mid s,a\right].$$
The vector $\theta_i$ contains current network weights, $\theta_{i-1}$ contains weights from the preceding iteration, and $\rho(s,a)$ is the behavior distribution over histories and actions. The target uses an immediate reward plus the best predicted continuation. Previous-iteration parameters are held fixed while optimizing one iteration, but targets still change across iterations because they are produced by the evolving network. This differs from ordinary supervised learning with labels fixed before training.

The optimizer figure isolates just one prerequisite: an update's step size affects whether parameters approach a minimum smoothly or oscillate. Its control changes the learning rate for 12 updates of the illustrative scalar quadratic $f(x)=x^2/2$, starting from $x=3$. Before changing the control, predict which learning rate reaches zero rapidly without overshooting.

The figure stops well short of the paper's training system. It uses plain one-dimensional gradient descent, whereas the Atari experiments used RMSProp with minibatches and a high-dimensional, moving Q-learning objective. Its trajectories are not empirical DQN learning curves and say nothing about Atari scores.

sections.title: Replay rewrites the order of experience
sections.markdown:
Online interaction produces a temporally ordered stream in which adjacent observations are strongly correlated. DQN changes the order in which that experience reaches the optimizer. At time $t$, it stores a transition
$$e_t=(s_t,a_t,r_t,s_{t+1})$$
in replay memory $\mathcal D$. Training updates then use random minibatches sampled from the retained pool rather than only the newest consecutive transitions. After the replay updates, the agent returns to the emulator and selects another action with an $\epsilon$-greedy behavior policy: it chooses a maximizing action with probability $1-\epsilon$ and a random action with probability $\epsilon$.

Consider three symbolic transitions $e_\alpha$, $e_\beta$, and a newly arriving $e_\gamma$. Storing $e_\gamma$ adds it to the same persistent pool as the earlier experiences. A uniform draw can then select $e_\alpha$ rather than the newest transition. Sampling copies the transition for an update; it does not remove it from replay. Consequently, a later minibatch may select $e_\alpha$ again. This reuse lets one interaction contribute to multiple weight updates, while drawing transitions out of temporal order weakens the strong adjacency correlations present in the original online stream.

Suppose the selected transition is the explicitly nonterminal
$$e_\alpha=(s_\alpha,a_\alpha,r_\alpha,s'_\alpha).$$
Its fields supply both sides of the sampled prediction error. Using the previous iteration's parameters, the network evaluates the legal actions at the recorded next state and forms
$$y_\alpha=r_\alpha+\gamma\max_{a'}Q(s'_\alpha,a';\theta_{i-1}).$$
In parallel, the current network evaluates the recorded state-action pair as $Q(s_\alpha,a_\alpha;\theta_i)$. A stochastic gradient step reduces the squared discrepancy
$$\left(y_\alpha-Q(s_\alpha,a_\alpha;\theta_i)\right)^2.$$
The continuation term appears because this example is nonterminal. The update changes the network parameters, but $e_\alpha$ remains a transition with the same state, action, reward, and next-state identity in replay.

This separation between the behavior that generated a transition and the greedy continuation used in its target makes the update off-policy. Stored experiences may come from exploratory actions or from older network parameters, whereas the target values the best currently represented continuation through the maximum over $a'$. Q-learning is therefore a natural match for replay. Mixing transitions produced by several earlier behavior policies also smooths abrupt shifts in the training distribution: a newly preferred action does not instantly make every update come from the states reached by that action.

The statistical benefits are limited by the replay rule actually used. The finite memory retains only the most recent $N$ experiences, so sufficiently old transitions are eventually overwritten. Uniform sampling gives every retained transition equal treatment, regardless of how surprising or informative its prediction error might be. Randomization reduces direct temporal correlation but does not make the samples independent, because transitions can share trajectories, policies, and visual situations. These limits matter operationally: rare useful experiences can disappear or be revisited no more often than routine ones, and correlated structure can remain in the training data. Replay nevertheless changes the learning problem in a precise way—it preserves a reusable pool of transition identities while decoupling the order of optimization updates from the order in which the agent encountered them.

sections.title: Turning recent pixels into every available choice
sections.markdown:
The preprocessing pipeline converts each raw RGB frame to grayscale, downsamples it to $110\times84$, and crops an $84\times84$ playing-area region. The function $\phi$ stacks the latest four processed frames, yielding an $84\times84\times4$ input. Multiple frames can reveal short-term motion that one still cannot, although four frames remain only a bounded approximation to the complete history.

The network first applies 16 convolutional filters of size $8\times8$ with stride 4 and rectifier nonlinearities. A second layer applies 32 filters of size $4\times4$ with stride 2, again followed by rectifiers. The final hidden layer is fully connected with 256 rectifier units. A linear output layer has one unit for each legal action; the games considered had between 4 and 18 valid actions.

Thus, for one processed history $\phi(s)$, a single forward pass produces $Q(\phi(s),a;\theta)$ for every action $a$. Shared convolutional computation extracts visual features once instead of requiring a separate full pass for each history-action pair. A greedy controller can then select the action with the largest output, while an $\epsilon$-greedy behavior policy sometimes explores.

The architecture does not reconstruct the emulator's true state, predict future frames, or explicitly model environment dynamics. It is model-free action-value prediction: observed transitions supply training samples, and the network directly maps recent visual evidence to estimates of future discounted reward.

sections.title: Seven games, three distinct comparisons
sections.markdown:
The experiments covered Beam Rider, Breakout, Enduro, Pong, Q*bert, Seaquest, and Space Invaders. Training used RMSProp, minibatches of 32, ten million frames, and replay memory containing the one million most recent frames. Training $\epsilon$ decreased linearly from 1 to 0.1 over the first million frames and stayed at 0.1 thereafter. Frame skip was 4 except in Space Invaders, where it was 3 because skip 4 made blinking lasers invisible. This was the reported hyperparameter exception.

Training rewards were clipped by sign: positive rewards became $1$, negative rewards became $-1$, and zero remained zero. This constrained derivative scale and helped reuse a learning rate across games, but it erased reward magnitude. A positive score change of 100 and one of 1 therefore generated the same clipped training reward for that step. Evaluation still used the real, unmodified games.

The result comparisons require careful separation. First, against Sarsa and Contingency—the two methods in the upper learned-method comparison—DQN's reported average score was higher on all seven games. Those averages used an $\epsilon$-greedy evaluation policy with $\epsilon=0.05$ for a fixed number of steps.

Second, HNeat was reported differently: its score was the highest-scoring single episode from deterministic policies, while DQN still used exploratory $\epsilon$-greedy sequences. The paper states that both DQN's average and maximum results exceeded HNeat on every game except Space Invaders. Therefore “all seven learning methods” would be false if it included HNeat; the defensible broader conclusion is six of seven under these nonidentical evaluation styles.

Third, relative to the paper's expert-human figures, DQN was reported above human performance on Breakout, Enduro, and Pong, close on Beam Rider, and far below on Q*bert, Seaquest, and Space Invaders. Average exploratory evaluations, best episodes, and human medians are different quantities and should not be silently merged.

sections.title: What the demonstration establishes—and what it cannot
sections.markdown:
The paper's central achievement is the integration of three mechanisms into one end-to-end control system. A convolutional network maps four processed Atari frames to one predicted action value per legal action. Experience replay retains observed transitions and presents randomized minibatches to the optimizer. Q-learning turns each sampled reward and next state into a bootstrapped target, allowing the network to learn about a greedy continuation even when the stored action came from exploratory or older behavior. Together, these mechanisms enabled one architecture and an almost identical training configuration to operate across seven games without hand-designed object features.

The evidence for stable training is empirical. Episode reward remained noisy because small parameter changes could alter the states visited by the policy and therefore the subsequent data distribution. As an additional diagnostic, the authors collected a fixed set of states before training and tracked the average, over those states, of the maximum predicted action value. That quantity rose more smoothly than average episode reward, and the reported experiments did not exhibit divergence. The consequence is appropriately modest: the training procedure worked stably in those seven runs under the reported conditions. A smooth increase in predicted $Q$ does not show that the predictions are calibrated to realized returns, does not ensure monotonic improvement in game score, and does not prove convergence of nonlinear off-policy Q-learning.

The method also compresses the information available to learning. Its four-frame input can expose short-term motion, but it cannot directly preserve every observation or action relevant to a strategy extending over many timesteps. The paper associates its largest human-performance gaps—on Q*bert, Seaquest, and Space Invaders—with strategies requiring long timescales. That interpretation is consistent with the bounded input representation, although the reported comparisons do not isolate four-frame history as the sole cause of those gaps.

Reward clipping introduces a different information loss. During training, every positive score change becomes $1$ and every negative score change becomes $-1$. This bounds the scale of error derivatives and supports reuse of one learning rate across games, but it makes rewards of the same sign indistinguishable in magnitude. As a result, the learned objective cannot prefer a 100-point event over a 1-point event merely because its immediate game-score change is larger. Evaluation on the unmodified games still measures the original scores, so easier optimization and fidelity to the game's scoring scale are in tension.

Replay has corresponding limits. Its finite capacity eventually overwrites older transitions, which can remove experiences that are no longer common under the current behavior. Uniform draws do not preferentially revisit transitions with unusually large errors or unusual outcomes. Random sampling weakens consecutive correlation and averages data over past behaviors, but residual dependence and a changing data distribution remain. These properties help explain why replay can improve data efficiency and reduce harmful feedback without supplying a theoretical guarantee.

Finally, the reported score comparisons answer several distinct questions. DQN's average $\epsilon$-greedy score exceeded Sarsa and Contingency on all seven games under the learned-agent evaluation protocol. The HNeat comparison used a highest-scoring deterministic episode, whereas DQN was evaluated with exploratory $\epsilon$-greedy control; DQN's average and maximum results were better on six games, with Space Invaders as the exception. Against the paper's expert-human figures, DQN scored higher on Breakout, Enduro, and Pong, close on Beam Rider, and far lower on Q*bert, Seaquest, and Space Invaders. Because averages, best episodes, exploratory policies, deterministic policies, and human medians are not interchangeable statistics, the strongest supported conclusion is specific: the paper demonstrated a broadly shared deep reinforcement-learning recipe with strong results across a seven-game testbed, while leaving convergence, long-horizon representation, and uniformly human-level control unresolved.

quiz.question: Why is Q-learning compatible with replaying transitions generated by exploratory or older behavior policies?

options.text: It is off-policy, so its greedy target can be learned from behavior that differs from the current greedy policy.
options.explanation: Correct: replayed actions need not have come from the policy currently being evaluated by the maximizing target.

options.text: It makes every replayed transition statistically independent.
options.explanation: Random sampling weakens direct temporal correlation but does not guarantee independence.

options.text: It converts four screens into the emulator's exact hidden state.
options.explanation: The internal state remains hidden; the frame stack is only a fixed-length history representation.
